candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis, Section XXXII.24. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13, ed. J. Gwynn / Schaff (1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'And Jacob was left alone; and there wrestled a man with him until the breaking of the day'. Ephrem reads the mysterious wrestler as the pre-incarnate Word — the same Person who later appears to Joshua as captain of the Lord's host (Josh 5:13-15) and who ultimately becomes incarnate in Mary's womb. Tewahedo Christology preserves the wrestling-with-the-pre-incarnate-Word as the canonical OT Christophany that establishes the principle: theophany in the OT is always the Son, never the Father.

candidates.source_attribution: Ephrem the Syrian, Commentary on Genesis, Section XXXII.28. NPNF Series 2, vol. 13, ed. J. Gwynn / Schaff (1898). PD.
candidates.draft_body:
Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Genesis (c. 360 AD)

'Thy name shall be called no more Jacob, but Israel: for as a prince hast thou power with God and with men, and hast prevailed'. Ephrem reads the new name as won-not-given: unlike Abraham's name change (simple divine declaration), Jacob WRESTLES for his new name. Tewahedo monastic-ascetical tradition uses this verse as the canonical warrant for spiritual struggle: some names (i.e., spiritual identities) are not handed over but must be wrested through prayer-as-combat. The monastic name received at tonsure is in this lineage.
